1.open: Think of a time someone gave you a second chance, or stood up for you when you hadn't earned it. What was that like?
questions: Paul opens with praise before he asks for anything. He says he hears of Philemon's "faith in the Lord Jesus and your love for all the saints" (v. 5). Why might it matter that Paul starts there? Who in your life needs to hear what you appreciate in them?

Paul says he could "order" Philemon but would rather "appeal on the basis of love" (vv. 8, 9). When is it easier to give an order than to make an honest appeal? How does it feel to be on the receiving end of each?

Onesimus was an enslaved man in Philemon's household, and Paul calls him "my child" whose father he became "while I was in chains" (v. 10). What does it tell you that Paul, a prisoner himself, cares so much about someone with so little standing in that world?
Paul writes that Onesimus was "useless" but is now "useful" (v. 11). The name Onesimus means "useful." What do you think Paul is doing with this wordplay, and how might it have landed with Philemon?

Paul wants Philemon to receive Onesimus "no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother" (v. 16). Christians differ on whether Paul is quietly hinting at freedom or asking for a new kind of relationship inside slavery. What do you notice in the text that makes you lean one way or the other?

Paul says, "charge it to my account" and "I will repay it" (vv. 18, 19). Where have you seen someone take on a cost that was not theirs to carry? What does that picture say to you about Jesus, or what do you find hard to believe about it?

Philemon has a real choice here, and Paul wants his goodness to come "by your own free will" (v. 14). Is there a relationship in your life where forgiving or welcoming someone feels costly? Be as honest as you like, including if you are not sure you can.
Paul is confident Philemon "will do even more than I ask" (v. 21), and the letter does not tell us what happened. How do you feel about an ending left open? What would you hope Philemon did?
1.life: Think of one person you have been holding at a distance because of something they did. This week, take one small step toward them: a message, a prayer for them by name, or a conversation you have been putting off.
1.prayer: Thank God for the grace that welcomes us when we have nothing to offer. Ask for the courage to receive others the same way, and pray for anyone in the group facing a hard relationship.
1.tip: Slavery is the hard spot. Some will be troubled that Paul does not openly demand freedom, and others will want a tidy answer. Name plainly that Christians read the letter differently, and that people on opposing sides once used it. Then keep the group on what the text clearly shows: Paul treats Onesimus as a beloved brother and asks Philemon to do the same.
